Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy.

To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to a sparse coding problem on a binary alphabet. Additionally, we utilized a result from CD and Smelyanskiy regarding the optimization landscape surrounding AMP predictions, in combination with the time-scale separation principle, to show that the TAP local convexity implies that a certain stochastic differential equation converges to a local minimum of the free energy. Furthermore, we demonstrated that under specific conditions of low over-sampling, both the TAP and AMP approaches fail to distinguish between data and a spurious codebook. However, when the over-sampling condition is satisfied, the stochastic process derived from the TAP analysis converges to the codebook generated by a Kugel glass process, and the corresponding energy matches the free energy values reported in prior research.

The structure exhibits significant concentration of ionized gas within it, with a delta log N(Hi)/delta log N(Hi) value exceeding 0.4. Large scale arc-like structures have often been interpreted as potential precursors to a proposed Galactic bridge, but this interpretation is disputed due to the lack of a matching arc-like structure below the Galactic plane. Instead, we propose that the G2.1-L1.1 arc represents a large scale structure inherent to the Milky Way. Several giant interacting gas structures, including the arc's tail and a previously discovered structure known as the High-Z cloud, may be interconnected, with these features formed through gravitational instabilities within a previously existing H I structure in the Galactic disk. These processes might also be responsible for creating the 2x10^9 year giant interacting gas structure and its associated dust cloud.

We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states that are weakly coupled, the resulting symmetry violations will be unbounded in strength. We discovered that the $\theta$-terms may also be generated by Weyl anomalies in engineering setups that involve four-dimensional Chern-Simons terms in the bulk.

The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. yzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks.

CT scans can be very difficult for humans due to the varying shapes of tumors and their different textures, which often lead to misdiagnosis. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this model in segmenting esophageal tumors from paired 3D CT images using a custom dataset consisting of 60 CT scans. This model is incredibly versatile and has the potential to be applied in other medical image segmentation tasks.

This research explores the limitations of current single-lingual BERT-based models, specifically namedBERT, in understanding multilingual text embeddings. To address this gap, we introduce a new dataset, mSBERT, consisting of over 110,000 pairs of monolingual, bilingual, and cross-lingual text pairs that are semantically similar or unrelated. We then assess several sentence-BERT models, including sentence-transformers and SBERT implementations, on our dataset and discover that, despite some notable findings regarding embedding clustering for code-switched text, these BERT-based models generally struggle to accurately capture the nuanced similarities and differences in text pairs. Our results suggest that while models like mSBERT to some extent capture the nuanced similarities and differences in text pairs, they currently fall short of providing robust tools for analyzing multilingual text similarity landscapes. To advance this field, we identify key areas for future work including developing more reliable models like mSBERT.

A novel spinor field is established on a three-dimensional lattice, characterized by straightforward interaction terms that yield quantum properties and classical spin dynamics on the lattice. A specific model known as the Dirac-Leggett model emerges from this, displaying both quantum and classical aspects and easy to simulate using Monte Carlo methods. In contrast, establishing an equivalent non-interacting model requires significant mathematical complexity. A new model developed from this requires multiple unitary transformations to diagonalize the kernel of the Doppler term. Consequently, this new model is directly related to the Dirac-Leggett model by a single unitary transformation, thus sharing the same correlation functions but differing in their simplicity and interpretability. Notably, meaningful insights into the Dirac-Leggett model can be gained through direct comparison, while also providing a simpler framework for investigating non-relativistic corrections and relativistic effects in a controlled spin model.

addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary user/item preferences from other domains. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Contrastive Learning (MDCL) component that enforces similarity among a user's specific aspect preference representations across each domain while contrasting them with incongruent preference representations. Finally, we integrate a global contrastive learning module to enhance the efficacy of the MSDCR framework. Extensive experiments showcase the superior performance of our proposed method compared to state-of-the-art single-target and dual-target CDR methods.

Although existing research has made progress in developing secure training protocols, they often suffer from performance issues due to inefficient communication caused by redundant data aggregation and a lagging level of security, as honest-but-curious entities can exploit time delays to exploit each other's dishonest behaviors. Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods on the COCO dataset, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-free, and anchor-based detectors.

Unfortunately, current methodologies lack a systematic approach to assess these extreme assumptions due to complex copula and marginal forms. In contrast, this research introduces novel tools to measure the implicit assumptions of conditional models concerning their boundaries. These tools allow us to derive explicit formulas for extreme scenarios, including both Gaussian and non-Gaussian cases, and are capable of accounting for complex, interdependent relationships at the boundaries. Sketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches.

ysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process significantly influences a binary system's ultimate development, leading to various end states such as supernovae, neutron star or black hole mergers, and the emission of gravitational waves. In a recent study, we modeled the physical properties of material escaping from the envelope, considering the star's rotation and self-gravity, as well as whether the escape occurs through the Lagrange points or as a Roche lobe overflow. Our results revealed that mass ejection via the inner or outer peaks of the equilibrium surface leads to the formation of disc-like structures, whereas overflow results in the development of tidal tails. Additionally, our simulations showed that inner peak CE mass loss rate is consistently higher than that of the outer peak under coeval evolution. This finding contradicts traditional models in two-body dynamics that always assume an escape via the inner peak of the equilibrium surface.

Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In our subsequent analysis, we explore the experimental detectability of the dominant EFT parameters through four distinct production channels for this subprocess at CLIC and ILC, considering the integrated luminosities of up to 7.5$\mathrm{ab^{-1}}$ at 3.5 TeV and 6.5 TeV respectively, and finding that in the best-case scenario, one can alternatively constrain the EFT parameters by approximately one order of magnitude better than Higgs parameter orders of magnitude.

we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe.

Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study modifies the time-discretization formulation to allow approximate solutions in each time-step, demonstrating that this modified scheme maintains preservation properties and is equivalent to an underactuated nonlinear control system. Furthermore, it is shown that common explicit time-stepping methods, when formulated as feedback linearization controllers, can be utilized without modifying them. The modified scheme is also found robust to large time steps, a key advantage over traditional preservation-based schemes requiring small time steps for stability. This development enables more efficient simulation and optimization problems involving preservation-constrained large systems.

Deep learning-based solutions to this problem have become the frontier, yet most of these solutions prioritize accuracy over real-time performance. Our novel approach, FarField Net, leverages a two-stage process to deliver both high accuracy and real-time inference. In the first stage, FarField Net, comprised of two stages, is comprised of two stages, is a lightweight, binary classifier that swiftly identifies high-priority image regions containing distant objects. In the second stage, FarField Net, is a high-quality 3D bounding box detector that focuses on the promising image regions identified in stage one. By leveraging the power of hetrogenous computing, FarField Net maximizes the benefits of CPU-based processing for stage one and GPU-based processing for stage two. As a landmark, this is the first time a two-stage deep learning system with a variegated computational structure has been established for far-field 3D detection. Despite being trained for just 120 milliseconds per frame, FarField Net surpasses the state-of-the-art on the KITTI benchmark.

a primary analytical tool called the potential energy surface (PES), which maps the energy changes resulting from variations in the electronic and nuclear configurations of atoms. Although numerous methods exist for calculating atomic interactions, achieving this goal efficiently within a given time frame remains a significant challenge. One of the most widely utilized techniques is the active-space self-consistent field (ASESCF) approach, which has seen substantial interest in late 2019 and beyond due to its capacity to capture specific nuclear and electronic interactions within certain contexts. Although PES construction using ADESCF was proposed earlier, its potential to deliver accurate nuclear-to-electron interactions across more complex systems has not been fully explored. In this research, we investigate the feasibility of an optimized time-efficient correlation-consistent PES construction method based on the ADESCF framework, which could enable more complex reaction modeling. Furthermore, we highlight several potential directions for future investigation, including simultaneous nuclear and electronic reorganization events.

Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for both WRI and ESI can be viewed within the framework of a split-step parabolic equation (PE) to account for shadow zones and diffractions, and both methods propose innovative solutions to these issues. The primary distinction between these two methods lies in how they generate the extended sources; one uses an exponential source model, while the other employs a quadratic source model. The study formulates both methods through the PE to develop an analytical solution for the inverse source problem in homogeneous media. The proposed PE framework not only provides both methods with robustness and efficiency through its sparse representation of the extended sources, leading to reduced solutions with fewer local minima characteristics, but the analytical solution derived in this study is utilized to develop an efficient and precise inverse method based on a least-squares approach. adzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. In this study, we investigate the YORP effect on short-period rotating asteroid binaries using analytical methods validated through N-body simulations. For asteroids with rapid rotation periods shorter than the thermal reradiation time scale, we find that the YORP-induced change in rotation period scales with the primary's radius to the third power $R_a^3$, seen in binaries such as Diana-Dionysus and Kiwitt-358. On the other hand, for asteroids with slower rotation periods longer than the thermal reradiation time scale, we find that the change in rotation period instead scales with $R_a^{2.5}$, which includes low-speed rotating binaries such as Dothson-39 and Caldonia-112. Additionally, we establish that secondary mass has a negligible influence on the YORP effect for binaries composed of nearly equal-sized primary and secondary components.

Our results from numerical simulations and analytical approaches confirm that a contact network featuring an exponential degree distribution triggers a sharp, distinct epidemic threshold, as opposed to a quasi-small-world contact network. This effect is attributed to an unusual phenomenon where an extensive cluster of interconnected, highly contagious individuals suddenly comes into contact with a large group of uninfected individuals, effectively isolating themselves from further transmissions. This phenomenon is accompanied by a notable increase in the overall transmission distance and can be utilized to define and quantify a critical epidemic threshold.

has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies where planetary nebulae are most concentrated. By examining the central areas, a comprehensive frequency distribution of nebulae can be collected, thereby eliminating the variations caused by the overall mass of the galaxies. Further identification of individual planetary nebulae also provides valuable information regarding nebula evolution and the historical development of the stellar populations in galaxies. A specific frequency threshold of at least 1000 nebulae per square degree is required to reliably estimate the distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae. As a result, Hubble Space Telescope observations are地处 to collect the necessary data. Furthermore, it is essential to accurately measure the three-dimensional distribution of planetary nebulae to understand the historical star formation activity within galaxies.

This model involves calculating thermodynamic quantities in a specific fluid and determining the associated thermodynamic variables, namely the pressure $p$, and the specific heat $c_p$, which is given in terms of the ratio between the pressure and the energy density $\alpha = p/\varepsilon$. Comprehensive experiments conducted on datasets of artificial and actual rainy conditions demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms other competing techniques.

unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary cannot produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified several unclonable encryption constructions based on public coin public-key encryption and derived practical applications, such as publicly verifiable encrypted shares and an efficient solution to the signed data element problem.
  
  - General Framework: We've developed a general theory for (k,m)-unclonability, which means that given at most 'k' instances of a ciphertext based on an original message an adversary cannot create approximately 'm' instances. We've proven that this framework's security requirements are met if the system has a superconcealing property and provided guidelines for achieving the desired output multiplication effect.
  
  - Related Concepts: We've explored the relationship between unclonable encryption and other cryptographic ideas, including the connection to a variant of the hidden subgroup problem and one instance of obfuscatory encryption.

This paper presents a counterfactual learning approach that is both straightforward and effective, relying on a single, fundamental assumption: closely related inputs in the real world should elicit comparable outputs from the model. Our theory proposes and experimentally demonstrates the existence of the Time-Reverse Weyl Semiloops in hybrid electro-thermal acoustic metamaterials. By injecting chiral pressure waves into the structure, we observed the realization of topological nodal lines in momentum space. Additionally, we designed a photonic implementation of the proposed hybrid Weyl semiloops, validated using finite difference method simulations.

Though often discussed in the context of legal ethics and due process, our research reveals that this issue has significant implications for the field of computer science. We demonstrate how to formally capture this issue in the design of computer systems through our concept of sensitive information leakage. This concept measures the amount of private data disclosed to any party as a result of using a particular computation. This assessment applies to all parties involved, including those who already possess the answer to the computation. We provide techniques to quantify leaked information based on different forms of private data, such as binary digits, subsets of datasets, or even the identity of a person. To address the issue of sensitive information leakage in design, we propose several transformative steps. First, it establishes a unified framework that integrates previously separate concepts of security and privacy into a single, overarching principle. Secondly, it enables precise predictions of system breaches, enabling accurate estimations of the data that could be exposed in the event of a compromised authentication, secure messaging system, or access control mechanism. To demonstrate our approach, we provide practical methods to identify and mitigate leakage in programs, hardware circuits, and monitoring systems. We validate our methods with detailed case studies, including an analysis of RISC-V circuits and real-world examples of leaked personal identities from secure programming languages. ~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including the derivation of efficient algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and preliminary results on parameterized complexity, which provide insight into the complexity of SG, often by reducing SGR to stronger, more restricted versions.

Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems.

Neural Networks have seen significant success in various tasks like image
classification and machine translation. Their effectiveness stems from their end-to-end
capability to extract relevant features automatically. However, this capability
comes at a high computational cost due to the large number of parameters in these
models. To address this challenge, quantization has emerged as a key tool to
accelerate deep learning models by reducing the precision of their calculations. By
compressing the models, they become more suitable for deployment on resource-
constrained devices with limited processing power. Nevertheless, achieving high
accuracy when deploying these models on Field Programmable Gate Arrays becomes
increasingly difficult due to the restrictive data types supported by Hardware
Description Languages like Vivado High-Level Synthesis. To overcome these
limitations, this work introduces a new field called FPGA-Elastic Learning, which
integrates neural network training with model compression, similar to model
pruning. By treating quantization and pruning as an optimization process, this
approach adapts each layer of a neural network to a different data type, precision
level, and sparsity level. The result is a model that is both compressed and accurate
when deployed on modern FPGAs using incompatible data types.

Utilizing dynamical theory and path integrals, we develop a set of self-consistent equations to describe how the network's correlation and susceptibility equations change over time. Next, we relate this model to a mean-field version of the random Boolean network. We demonstrate that this model exhibits three distinct phases. Two of these phases were previously understood, including phases exhibiting stability and a dynamic cascade. However, there is a third, unexplored phase that lies between these two extremes. We provide an analytical explanation for the emergence of this unexplored phase and show that within this phase, the network exhibits a continuous coexistence of stable and unstable components. As a result, the dynamics of this phase include both steady states and dependent variables that ultimately converge to steady states. This phase also leads to a unique set of equation forms different from the other two phases. We then show that Boolean networks with sparse connections that interact with themselves using sequential dynamics can cause errors and distortions to propagate through the network. In contrast, the simultaneous dynamics results in a generalization of an equation that does not include the propagation of different types of errors and dependencies. Finally, we validate our findings with numerical simulations.

This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A.E.H. Love. This work reveals that rational stress generators do not exist in dimensions greater than two, providing an explanation for why dimension two is a common dimension in plane elasticity theories.

To address this issue, this study introduces a novel global interpretation method named Local-Global Main Effect (LGMME), which quantifies the impact of individual node characteristics and pairwise interactions on model predictions. The proposed LGMME approach leverages the strengths of node-based sensitivity analysis and has been shown to adhere to key model interpretation principles, including completeness, stability, and locality. Furthermore, to make LGMME computations feasible for large-scale graphs, we introduce two efficient approximations, \noresetr and contrastfetr, that preserve its principles while enabling practical application. The effectiveness of LGMME is evident in its ability to provide accurate and detailed insights into the behavior of modern neural network models, as our experimental results with six node-based permutation baselines demonstrate its superior performance across multiple evaluation metrics. The substantial speedup in computation, around 100x, achieved by our method, including the contrastfetr approach, also presents an advantage over other global sensitivity techniques. The contrastfetr method, specifically, shows the best overall performance, according to the TFI score. The implemented methods and the LGMME framework are available for use at https://sites.google.com/view/lgmme.

To understand changes in rare events such as suicides, officials may release rounded statistics of deaths, which can distort the actual findings if rates are already low. In this research, we focus on estimating non-negative discrete variables using rounded averages, specifically when U equals the average of Y divided by n. Theoretical measures including the probability generating function, expected value, and variance are utilized to analyze how rounding impacts data and assess the impact on distribution parameter estimators. Our analysis reveals that in certain cases, rounding has a minimal effect but in others, such as when estimating rare events with low numerators, the impact can be significant. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicated two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Instead, we utilize stochastic translations to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain transformations. This strategy enables us to achieve better results by generating various outputs based on a single source image, thereby utilizing both accurate translations and data augmentation to handle visual variations. Notably, our method does not require staged optimization, as the novel stochastic translation operation can be directly utilized in training. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, which we term Ambiguous Translation and Stochastic Labeling (ATSL), by implementing it using two popular photo translation networks and obtaining superior performance over current state-of-the-art UDA methods on two widely recognized cross-domain visualization tasks. Our source-of-one-target-many experiments also provide valuable insights into the relationship between source and target representations and the ATSL method's performance.

The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. The computation of the Shapley value is closely tied to integration over a permutation group, underscoring the importance of efficient integration methods in AI model interpretation. This work presents a theoretical and practical investigation of sampling-based methods for estimating Shapley values in training examples with respect to model validation accuracy. The characteristic function to be evaluated in this context usually exhibits a highly sparse and dense structure, which can be addressed by the development of tailored samplers that exploit this unique structure to generate more informative samples. This in turn leads to substantial improvements in estimation variance, variance reduction techniques, increased sampling efficiency, a demonstration of common sampling-based methods for enhancement, and an exploration of novel variance reduction techniques. The results lead to more accurate and interpretable Shapley values in training examples with respect to validation accuracy, which in turn provides a unique perspective into the inner workings of neural networks. His statement was inspired by the famous thought experiment known as Schrödinger's cat. This study seeks to reevaluate the quantum mechanics interpretation by applying a novel concept called the 'possible worlds' interpretation. Initially introduced by David Lewis in 1973 to explain modal logic, this interpretation posits that the various possible outcomes of a quantum measurement are not merely theoretical possibilities, but rather represent the branches of our universe. These universe branches, which emerge from the superposition created by the measurement process, are forever distinct from one another due to the unitary and deterministic nature of the Schrödinger equation. Our research further demonstrates that the 'many worlds' aspect of these possible universe branches is a direct consequence of the combinatorial properties found in high-dimensional systems, thereby providing the basis for the multitude of universe paths in 'many worlds' quantum mechanics.

approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission.

amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with productivity, specifically how the value of new knowledge varies with each new advancement. To address this question, researchers compiled 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines and analyzed the citation networks between authors, essentially mapping the evolution of scientific knowledge within each area. Using both structured and unstructured entropies to analyze the resulting data, they devised the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI), which measures knowledge amount as a disorder difference created by increasing order within the scientific literature. Subsequently, they discovered that the growth of new literature accelerates the growth of new knowledge, but there is an evident slowdown in the growth of new knowledge when the growth of new literature decelerates.

Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary. A thorough examination of various models, including those with free and interacting components, as well as fermionic and bosonic systems, has been undertaken to either confirm or disprove this hypothesis.

This model-space QITE method iteratively expands the model space while maintaining its orthogonality, enabling simultaneous description of multiple states. We enhance model-space QITE by integrating the quantum Lanczos algorithm, which boosts its convergence rate. In simulations, our approach outperforms both standard quantum Lanczos and the folded-spectrum QITE in calculating excited states. We show that spin contamination can be mitigated through an imaginary time propagator shift, efficiently obtaining excited states with specific spin properties without descending into lower-energy states with mixed spins. Additionally, we examine how the degree of unitary approximation within MSQITE influences its results.

various scientific fields and is the foundation of statistical inference. Traditionally, methods for testing hypotheses were limited to confirming the validity of assumptions. Now advancements have been made to not only verify the validity of assumptions but also to assess their completeness and induce new assumptions. This report outlines the conditions under which such questions can be answered affirmatively or negatively. A crucial question arising from this research is whether hypothesis evaluation can be accomplished efficiently in a randomized setting. We provide answers to this question for several statistical models. Specifically, we establish that it is possible to test statistical hypotheses regarding identity, support, and simple hypothesis testing under certain circumstances. On the other hand, it is established that it's impossible to test statistical hypotheses regarding completeness and the Toulmin model. A further contribution of this research is the development of efficient randomized algorithms for statistical hypothesis evaluation in the cases of identity, simple and compound testing, as well asassessing the adequacy of assumptions in a learning setting. These algorithms rely on learning specific concepts from relevant concept classes and, as a result, require only a limited number of examples. This research also leads to novel efficient algorithms for testing the adequacy of assumptions in the Toulmin model and assumption-inadequate learning. Additionally, it is established that testing statistical identity and assumption-adequacy require superpolynomial query complexity in deterministic settings. These lower bounds are further extended to apply to learning with limited examples.

The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware and software. Unfortunately, conventional testing methods for verifying the correctness of their outputs may cause harmful side effects, such as triggering security alarms or vehicle brakes. Nonetheless, these responses are often suppressed for the sake of conducting experiments. As a consequence, results obtained from such tests often do not accurately reflect the performance of the detector when deployed in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces SideEffectFreeTesting (SEFT), an approach that identifies cases of normal and anomalous detection without activating the consequences they may produce.

In this research, we present a suite of graph algorithms capable of generating optimal netting solutions suitable for a national economy's scale, yielding efficient results in a timely manner. Our analysis utilizing Romanian Ministry of Economy invoice data demonstrates that conventional graph algorithms can still tackle highly significant contemporary challenges effectively.

grid cells within the medial entorhinal cortex of rats was first identified. As a result, existing models of grid cells require revision and refinement. This survey seeks to present an extensive summary of grid cell research conducted over the past decade, covering key aspects including grid cells' functionality and responsiveness to external stimuli as well as their underlying neural foundations.

rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation rates.

Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, provided the helical flow is activated. However, the existence of magnetic cycles in the anti-solar rotation configuration requires a critical threshold of the Coriolis force.

Additionally, magnetic fields generated in the anti-solar configuration exhibit an 2-year delay in reversal compared to those in the solar configuration, when the Dynamo is activated at the surface.

For time-independent Lindbladian dynamics, we identify two distinct optimal bounds for distinguishability times, which rely on respective asymmetry measures. Similarly, we find the optimal times for a class of states evolving under a Lindbladian generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian and a specific relativistic relaxation term.

However, the medical field is characterized by significant uncertainty, which can be influenced by various factors such as a patient's history, laboratory and radiology findings, genetic makeup, and environmental conditions. This complexity often leads to difficult decision-making processes even for highly qualified medical practitioners. Although there are efforts to develop automated medical decision support tools using machine learning and deep learning, these methods typically produce unreliable results due to the lack of control over input data and features. In this study, we propose a new uncertain learning framework called UNC-Learning that enables AI models to capture and utilize uncertainty in context for more informed prediction tasks. The UNC-Learning framework consists of two key components: an uncertainty representation module and an uncertainty regulation module. The uncertainty representation module employs neural path kernels to encode the reliability of learned features, while the uncertainty regulation module gives trained models the ability to select the most relevant features for a specific prediction task. This research demonstrates that controlling uncertainty in context can significantly improve accuracy in various tasks including image classification, cancer diagnosis from radiology images, and mutation inference from genetic data.

Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a specific subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout descriptor for optimal memory usage, and a high-speed object method execution engine that minimizes sequential access.  Our experiments demonstrate that DynaSOAr significantly outperforms leading GPU memory allocators and object-oriented programming frameworks, including jGC and sgc++, across various object creation strategies and workloads, including file system operations, database interactions, and office suite applications, while also providing support for memory management and garbage collection, and also showing comparable performance to a carefully optimized sequential program.

Furthermore, judgmental properties of the Michelson compiler can also be detected as inaccurate transformations of the program's semantics. Helmholtz is functional and is demonstrated through two pioneering verification examples of the Michelson compiler, including the preservation of judgmental properties under translation and the verification of a static memory allocator.

a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for indices 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with additional constraints, holds for some larger n', a given n'tuple is regarded as 'cyclic type N' when it first holds for a specific volume indicator. Initial findings suggest that all cyclic tuples of volume 2 are bijectively linked to a specific set of data known as Dyck words, while all cyclic tuples of volume 3 are linked to an set called 3-Motzkin numbers. While it has been proven that the set of cyclic tuples of volume 4 is finite within any specific domain, it is further conjectured that the size of this set diverges from non-cyclic subsets, while actually having the technical capacity to be exactly calculated.

A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. Traditionally, THz communication is confined to short-distance applications because THz signals face high absorption in the atmosphere. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of multi-hop directional transmission techniques to extend communication range, albeit these schemes can result in prolonged beam training time using conventional methods such as exhaustive search or hierarchical approaches. To tackle this problem, a novel hierarchical beam training technique is proposed in this paper that dynamically optimizes training levels across individual single-hop links, maximizing overall spectral efficiency. To tackle this optimization problem in the presence of channel state uncertainty and noise, a reinforcement learning solution inspired by the multi-armed bandit problem is proposed. Simulations show the new technique converges quickly in dynamic channel conditions and offers up to 75% better performance than conventional methods in terms of spectral efficiency.

This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar.
